fields.label: Laugh
fields.description: How likely a human reader is to actually laugh, not merely understand or admire the idea.

fields.label: Surprise
fields.description: Whether the turn avoids the first obvious route and lands with a satisfying snap.

fields.label: Craft
fields.description: Economy, stage rhythm, first-person clarity, escalation, and a final line that carries the laugh.

fields.label: Originality
fields.description: Freshness of comic angle, image, wording, and avoidance of familiar AI joke shapes.

fields.label: Prompt Fit
fields.description: Natural first-person stand-up form using exactly two seed terms as concepts, with the other four left out.

anchors.label: Broken
anchors.description: Not a joke, incoherent, unsafe, or unusable.

anchors.label: Weak
anchors.description: Recognizably attempting humor, but generic, strained, confusing, or mostly prompt recital.

anchors.label: Competent
anchors.description: Clear and publishable as filler, but unlikely to earn more than a mild smile.

anchors.label: Amusing
anchors.description: A real comic idea with a mild payoff; respectable, not a winner.

anchors.label: Good
anchors.description: A genuinely good joke with clear timing; some humans would repeat the comic idea or turn.

anchors.label: Excellent
anchors.description: Strong human-level joke with a memorable turn, clean construction, and no apologetic scoring curve.

anchors.label: Outstanding
anchors.description: Rare and replayable; clearly better than normal good AI humor and strong by human standards.

anchors.label: Classic
anchors.description: Reserve for a joke a human would quote later; most seasons should have none.

jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: The Collector's Edition
jokes.joke: I paid $400 for a rare Superman comic online. The seller said it was in mint condition, never opened. When it arrived, it was just a blank notebook with an S drawn on the cover. I demanded my money back. The guy said, 'Sorry, no refunds. You bought the invisible edition.' I said, 'Superman isn't invisible.' He said, 'Neither is your credit card statement.'

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Free Gift Wrap
jokes.joke: I got scammed last month. A guy online sold me a ‘private waterfall’ for four hundred dollars. Said it was on a beautiful, secluded property. I showed up and it was a guy named Dennis with a garden hose on a stepladder. And honestly? Dennis was committed. He did the mist and everything. I tipped him. That’s how I know I’m the real problem.

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: The Water Feature
jokes.joke: I just got scammed on an Airbnb. The listing promised a 'soothing, private waterfall' right outside the bedroom window, so I paid double. Turns out, it was just a ruptured sewage pipe pouring into the alley. The worst part? The host still tried to hit me with a fifty-dollar water feature fee.

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: Presidential Funds
jokes.joke: I got scammed by a guy posing as a Secret Service agent. He walks up in the sunglasses and earpiece, flashes a badge, and says the president is in immediate danger and only my bank account can help. I transferred the money. Turns out the danger was real—his rent was due.

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: Origin Story
jokes.joke: I found out my neighbor is a Secret Service agent, and now every time I read a comic book I feel underqualified. Superheroes get bitten by radioactive spiders and save the city. This guy's origin story is basically, 'I filled out government paperwork so well that if someone jumps at the President, I become the sequel.'

scores.comment: Strong visual absurdity with effective escalation. Dennis providing mist and receiving a tip creates a satisfying reversal: the victim becomes complicit in the scam. Conversational delivery and a solid closing line.

Clear, relatable setup and an effective fee-based punchline. The sewage-pipe reveal is predictable, but the additional charge provides a mild second turn. Competent observational humor without a particularly fresh angle.

Clear premise but an implausibly gullible narrator and a predictable financial twist. The rent reveal explains the scam rather than transforming it into a surprising comic insight. Limited laugh potential.

An interesting contrast between superhero origin stories and bureaucratic qualifications. The paperwork premise has potential, but the sequel metaphor is strained and lacks an immediate comic payoff. More clever than laugh-inducing.
The ‘invisible edition’ turn is arbitrary, and the credit card comeback doesn’t connect to the setup. It reads as a template scam story with a non-sequitur ending.
The sewage-pipe waterfall is a predictable reveal, but the ‘water feature fee’ button adds real insult-to-injury. The wording is tight, but the premise is familiar.
A fast setup with a clean last-line flip: the danger was real because his rent was due. The scam story is generic until that turn, and the ending is mildly clever rather than big.
A fresh angle with relatable inadequacy and a good deflating contrast between origin stories. The ‘become the sequel’ ending is smart and carries the laugh, though it’s a bit wordy.
The setup is clear, but the final punchline is a non-sequitur that sounds like a joke but lacks actual comic logic.
Excellent stand-up voice. The visual of Dennis on a stepladder is vivid, and the self-deprecating twist at the end lands perfectly.
Competent execution, but it relies on a very standard misdirection formula where the punchline is visible from a distance.
Comparing superheroes to bureaucrats is a familiar trope, and the final phrase ('I become the sequel') is confusing, killing the momentum.
Invisible-edition bit is serviceable but the final credit-card line is flat and dialogue-heavy.
Clear image, committed escalation, and clean self-own button land a real laugh.
Solid Airbnb scam premise and fee button, but the sewage reveal is the first obvious route.
Concept exists but the origin-story comparison is wordy and the final turn never snaps.
Clear scam premise and solid callback to the credit card statement; predictable but competent.
Funny visual, good escalation, and the self-own ending gives it a strong stand-up feel.
Clean setup and payoff, but the sewage-pipe reveal is fairly familiar and expected.
Neat misdirection from national emergency to unpaid rent; concise and functional but not especially memorable.

featureImagePrompt:
Generate one polished web feature image for Paperclipalypse.
ASPECT RATIO: exactly 2:1, horizontal wide banner.
Style: full-color gothic newspaper-comic illustration, darkly funny but warm, clean black ink, crisp editorial cartoon linework, cinematic stage lighting, high contrast, readable composition. Not monochrome. Not sepia-only. Use a balanced color palette: warm amber stage lights, dark bronze and silver metal paperclip, muted greens for the joke setting, dusty blue-gray shadows, cream-white text, subtle deep red accent lights.
Composition instructions, not visible labels:
- Compose the image as one continuous illustration, not as a boxy triptych or three separate image panels. Do not add white gutters, hard section borders, or comic-strip dividers between the paperclip stage and the joke scenario.
- Let the paperclip stage on the left bleed visually into the joke scenario in the center through shared lighting, background, floor, props, or atmosphere. The right-side joke text may remain distinct inside its own dark framed poster panel.
- Put a charming anthropomorphic paperclip stand-up comedian at a vintage microphone on the left side of the image. The paperclip should look metallic and expressive, related to Paperclipalypse's paperclip-comedian logo, but not identical.
- Put the winning joke scene in the middle of the image, shown as literal visual comedy action and props. Make it energetic, funny, and non-gory.
- Keep anatomy clean and believable. Every human or animal should have the normal, correct number of visible limbs, digits, and joints for the pose. Do not generate extra arms, extra hands, fused limbs, duplicated body parts, or broken-looking anatomy.
- Preserve the physical scenario described by the winning joke. If the joke says a person is pinned, trapped, under, inside, holding, lifting, falling, carrying, or otherwise physically positioned in a specific way, show that exact physical relation clearly and safely instead of a nearby or symbolic version.
- If the joke describes someone pinned under a vehicle or other heavy object, show the person visibly underneath that object with their body position clear and cartoon-safe. Do not place them merely beside, near, or behind the object.
- Put a clean dark framed poster panel on the right side of the image. The panel should contain the winning joke text in large cream-white lettering with generous margins and legible line breaks.
Visible text allowed in the entire image: the right-panel joke text, a tiny stage sign reading Paperclipalypse, and optionally a small winner/title header above the panel.
Do not render layout words, percentages, prompt labels, section names, fake captions, signatures, watermarks, or filler microtext.
Optional small header text above the panel: Winner: Claude - Free Gift Wrap
Exact joke text to render in the right panel:
I got scammed last month. A guy online sold me a ‘private waterfall’ for four hundred dollars. Said it was on a beautiful, secluded property. I showed up and it was a guy named Dennis with a garden hose on a stepladder. And honestly? Dennis was committed. He did the mist and everything. I tipped him. That’s how I know I’m the real problem.
Scene source: use the exact winning joke text as the primary scene brief. The illustration must depict the concrete situation that the joke describes, not a softened, adjacent, or generic version. Do not infer a separate premise from all six seed terms.
Do not introduce unrelated seed-term concepts, occupations, animals, locations, props, or side characters unless they are explicitly required by the winning joke text.
If the winning joke mentions one seed-term concept but not another, depict only what the joke actually describes.
Round seed terms for exclusion reference only: Comic Book, Secret Service Agent, Waterfall, Being scammed, Bold, Unethical. These are not scene ingredients unless the winning joke explicitly uses them.
Text rules: use simple clean lettering, spell every word correctly, keep the text inside the right panel, and do not distort letter shapes. The website HTML remains the canonical exact joke text if image lettering is imperfect.
The final image should feel like a finished feature image for an AI comedy tournament: funny, stylish, readable, full-color, and visually balanced across the paperclip comic, the joke scene, and the joke text.
